item.title: Mamdani to release documents on 9/11 health impacts before 25th anniversary
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Tuesday that his administration will release more than 170,000 pages of documents shedding new light on the air quality around Ground Zero in the months following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

In a press conference at the City Hall Rotunda, Mamdani said these documents would only be the first release of information that will reveal new details about "what the city knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it and how they acted to limit liability."

Over the next year, hundreds of thousands of more documents will be released on a public portal that will be freely accessible to every New Yorker, Mamdani said.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

item.title: Congress spends $7 trillion. Here’s how that math works out if you think of just $100
item.description: A breakdown of how Washington spends every $100 shows Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid and debt interest consume most of federal spending.
item.content:encoded:
You work. You get paid. Washington takes its cut. But have you ever stopped to ask one simple question: Where does the money actually go?

Forget trillion-dollar numbers for a minute. Most Americans can't comprehend the difference between $1 trillion and $7 trillion anyway. Let's shrink Washington down to something we all understand: a $100 bill.

In fiscal year 2025, the federal government spent roughly $7 trillion. Social Security alone consumed about $1.6 trillion. Major federal health programs, including Medicare and Medicaid, were another enormous piece. Defense approached $900 billion.

WASHINGTON IS DRIVING AMERICA TOWARD A DEBT CRISIS WE CAN'T IGNORE ANY LONGER

And then there's the number that should make every taxpayer spit out their morning coffee: interest.

The federal government spent about $970 billion just on net interest on the national debt. Not roads. Not teachers. Not soldiers. Not Social Security checks.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS HAVE LOTS OF IDEAS, BUT HOW ARE WE SUPPOSED TO PAY FOR THEM?

Interest.

That means roughly $14 out of every $100 Washington spent went toward interest on money we've already borrowed.

‘THE ODYSSEY’ REMINDS US OF THE NIGHTMARE WE ARE LEAVING FOR AMERICAN CHILDREN

Think about your own household budget. Imagine earning $100 and immediately throwing $14 in the fireplace because of credit-card balances you accumulated years ago.

You'd probably say you have a spending problem. Washington calls it a budget.

JOHN ADAMS MADE A TERRIFYING PREDICTION. AMERICA IS CLOSE TO PROVING HIM CORRECT

So where did the rest go?

Roughly speaking, out of every $100 the federal government spent in 2025, about $23 went to Social Security, approximately $26 went toward major health programs, around $13 went toward national defense, and about $14 serviced the interest on our debt. The remaining dollars funded everything from veterans' benefits and income-security programs to transportation, education, federal agencies and thousands of other government programs.

You can argue all day about which of those programs are worthwhile. But here's the part Washington doesn't put on your receipt.

We didn't have the $100.

BILLIONAIRE BEZOS SUGGESTS NO TAXES FOR HALF THE NATION. IS THAT CRAZY OR OVERDUE?

Federal revenues were only about $5.2 trillion while spending approached $7 trillion. The result was another roughly $1.8 trillion deficit in fiscal 2025. In other words, for every $100 Washington spent, it collected only about $74 and borrowed roughly $26 to make up the difference.

Try that financial plan at your house. Earn $74. Spend $100. Put the other $26 on the credit card. Then do it again next year. And the year after that.

SIX DIFFERENT WAYS THAT PROVE THE WEALTHY PAY A LOT MORE THAN THEIR ‘FAIR SHARE’

Eventually, your banker is going to have a conversation with you that nobody in Congress seems interested in having.

This isn't a Republican problem or a Democratic problem. It's an American math problem.

WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD

Politicians love telling you about the benefits they're going to protect, the programs they're going to create and the taxes somebody else is supposedly going to pay. Nobody likes telling you the truth.

We have promised ourselves a government we aren't currently willing to pay for. And taxpayers should demand something that every restaurant, grocery store and hardware store already gives us.

A receipt.

Every year, Americans should be able to see exactly how Washington spent every $100 it collected and how much additional money it borrowed in our name.

Because here's the number that scares me most.

The Congressional Budget Office says net interest costs are projected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026 and could reach about $2.1 trillion annually by 2036 under current law.

That's not a rounding error.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That's money future taxpayers will send to Washington before Congress buys them a single bridge, missile or Medicare benefit. Americans argue constantly about whether our taxes are too high or too low. Maybe we're asking the wrong question.

Before Washington asks Americans for another dollar, taxpayers should be asking: What did you do with the last $100?

item.title: Fox News Power Rankings: What’s in an economy?
item.description: Trump's economy approval sits at -33 points, but Democrats' competing visions on cost of living and inflation haven't won voters over either.
item.content:encoded:
Eight weeks from today, millions of Americans will choose their next congressperson. Poll after poll tells us that the state of the economy will shape their choice: it’s the top issue for voters by a wide margin and most Americans are in a sour mood about it.

That’s not the end of the story.

We’ve learned from previous elections that voters consider a wide range of issues when they vote. The "economy" has different meanings to voters. Optimism doesn’t win over voters on pocketbook issues. And this year, while voters aren’t happy with President Donald Trump’s economy, that hasn't yet made them enthusiastic about the Democratic alternative.

These are the four rules to think about as we inch closer to the midterms.

Meantime, Democrats inch closer to victory as the Power Rankings takes a fresh look at congressional races in Missouri and Ohio.

The importance of the economy to elections has been a golden rule since the early '90s, when Democratic strategist James Carville famously cited "the economy, stupid" as the most important focus for a campaign.

Did you know it was only one of three orders he gave to candidates that cycle?

The economy has been a top-three issue throughout the Trump era, including the last two midterm elections, where it was the most important issue for 47% of voters (2022) and 18% of voters (2018).

If that 2018 figure feels low, it’s because healthcare (26%) and immigration (23%) finished ahead. That year, Republicans lost 42 seats.

No wonder another of Carville’s three rules for candidates was "don’t forget health care." (The third was "change vs more of the same.")

HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY'

The state of the economy bleeds into other major concerns, including healthcare. But even a strong economy wasn’t enough to get the GOP out of that election unscathed. And healthcare looms as another important issue this year: it’s ranked close behind the economy in most surveys this year.

When pollsters ask about voters’ views on the economy, they usually ask how important "the economy" or "the state of the economy" is, or whether they’re satisfied with Trump’s performance on that issue.

In some important ways, Trump has a strong economic record. Just last week, the U.S. added 162,000 jobs, about triple what economists had expected. The unemployment rate was steady at 4.1%. The stock market also continues to grow, even as Iran and tariffs drive volatility.

These have helped keep Trump’s overall economic approval rating in the low-to-mid 30s in multiple polls this summer.

When pollsters ask only about Americans’ personal economic situation, things look tougher.

TRUMP'S APPROVAL RATING PLUMMETS TO NEW LOW AHEAD OF CRITICAL MIDTERMS: 'MORE WORK TO DO'

In a Reuters/Ipsos poll released last week, 32% of voters said they approved of Trump on the economy. But only a quarter approved of his performance on cost of living and 24% approved of him on inflation and prices.

The costs of gas, food and other basic goods are the major factors driving this discrepancy. If Democrats deliver a strong result in November, it will come down to a presidential approval rating in the mid-20s on these issues.

In 2022, President Joe Biden faced similar headwinds: the economy was rebounding, especially if you looked at unemployment, but inflation hovered around the 8% mark all year. Gas prices came in around $3.75.

The Biden administration kept selling the positives. First, inflation was "transitory." Then the president argued that "zero percent inflation" from one month to another was a win, despite the high annualized rate. Senior officials took victory laps on the unemployment rate.

Voters rejected this messaging at the ballot box, delivering the House to the GOP after a net loss of nine Democratic seats and handing Biden a net approval rating of -23 points on the economy.

Today, headline inflation is less than half that at 3.4%, while gas prices are a little higher at $4.15. Trump’s net approval on the economy currently sits at -33 points.

The Trump administration is running a familiar playbook. Vice President JD Vance said last week that gas prices could be worse if not for the Trump administration. As Fox’s Gillian Turner noted on "Special Report," there are similarities between a comment like that and the statements Biden officials made four years earlier.

These optimistic visions are likely to remain a tough sell to voters.

It’s easy to look at all this and think the Democrats are in for a big night in November. That’s certainly a possibility.

But polls keep showing that voters are just as discouraged by the left’s economic messaging.

FOX NEWS POLL: MOST RATE THE ECONOMY NEGATIVELY, INCLUDING HALF OF REPUBLICANS

Right now, Democrats are offering voters competing economic visions. Some, like Abdul El-Sayed and Troy Jackson, want a revolution that starts with "Medicare-for-all" and higher taxes on the wealthy. Others say they want to undo Trump’s agenda while keeping the core of America’s economic system in place.

It’s not yet clear whether these visions are unappealing to voters or whether the contrast between them is the problem.

Either way, in the Reuters/Ipsos survey, 36% of voters say Republicans are the better party to handle the economy, while 37% prefer the Democrats. The poll has a ±3.3pt margin of error.

That’s not encouraging for Team Blue.

If the Republicans hold relatively steady in November – also a possibility in this forecast – those results will explain why.

Democrats are still the favorites to take the House this November, with 212 seats in their columns to the GOP’s 206. There are 17 seats that are so close they could go either way.

Those seats tend to swing in one direction as votes get counted. On a good night for Democrats, that means 229 seats, while a good night for the GOP would still see them hold onto their current House majority.

(A "great" night for either party would mean winning some of the seats that lean toward the opponent in this forecast. The Power Rankings puts seats in the "lean" category when they’re highly competitive, but one party has an edge.)

The changes in this forecast, which see two seats fall out of the GOP’s columns, all come from Missouri and Ohio.

Republicans picked up redistricting wins across the southeast after the Supreme Court’s ruling narrowing the scope of the Voting Rights Act this year.

That includes Missouri, where Republican lawmakers redrew the Kansas City-based 5th District, currently held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver, who won re-election there by 24 points, to include more White, rural areas.

That put the district into the Solid R column in the initial Power Rankings this year.

Last Thursday, the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously blocked the new districts from being used unless voters approve them in a referendum. The order restores the state’s existing map, flipping Cleaver’s district back to Solid D.

MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP

(It also makes Missouri’s 2nd District more competitive. The rankings already had that district at Likely R; we’re keeping it there for now.)

Missouri has appealed the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court, which could rule on the state ruling quickly. For now, Cleaver holds on to the 5th District.

Three races in Ohio are heading leftward.

First, Ohio’s 7th District, held by Republican Max Miller. The congressman’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused Miller of physically abusing both her and their young daughter. Miller denies the allegations and has suggested Moreno has mental health issues.

Moreno is the daughter of Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, who Miller says is trying to take down his political career.

The 7th District was already close for the ‘likely’ column, and after these headlines and some prodding from Republicans to drop out, it’s become highly competitive. It moves from Likely R to Toss Up.

Meanwhile, in the southwest of the state, watch the 10th and 15th Districts, held by Republicans Mike Turner and Mike Carey, respectively.

These shouldn’t be part of the Democratic playbook in a regular election year: they’re predominantly White and middle-class.

Turner’s 10th District contains Dayton and some suburban areas; Carey’s 15th includes some suburban and exurban parts around Columbus and stretches to the rural south.

As the Fox News Poll has shown twice now, Democrat Sherrod Brown is running a strong race for Senate; up eight points at 53% in May and August. That kind of performance could create a closer race than Republicans would like.

The "Mikes" have the clear advantage, but victory isn’t a sure thing. The 10th and 15th Districts move from Solid R to Likely R.

item.title: Trey McKinney says Bassmaster veterans made him earn their respect before historic AOY season
item.description: Trey McKinney broke Kevin VanDam's 1992 record as the youngest Bassmaster Angler of the Year, but earning Elite Series respect was no small task.
item.content:encoded:
Trey McKinney has spent most of his professional fishing career being the youngest guy in the room.

And apparently, the Bassmaster Elite Series veterans weren't exactly waiting at the dock with open arms.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

McKinney arrived on the Elite Series as a teenager and immediately started making noise. Now, at just 21 years old, he's already a former Rookie of the Year, the youngest Elite Series winner in history and, as of last weekend, the youngest Bassmaster Angler of the Year ever.

But according to McKinney, earning all those accolades was one thing. Earning the respect of the other Elites took a little longer.

"They're not a very welcoming crew to begin with," McKinney told OutKick OutDoors. "If you're somebody that's coming on the Elite Series, don't expect a warm hand of, 'Come on, buddy. The water's warm. Come on in. It's a great time.'"

McKinney isn't complaining about it. In fact, he thinks that's probably how it should be.

"Rookies coming in, you get a hard time. You've got to learn how to prove yourself," he said. "And once you do that, it honestly makes it that much sweeter."

Watch Trey McKinney's full interview with OutKick OutDoors here:

For McKinney, proving himself happened quickly on paper. He finished second in the Angler of the Year standings in each of his first two Elite seasons, both times behind Chris Johnston.

But he said the first couple of years were still a "hard road" when it came to being accepted by the veterans around him.

"This year, it's kind of watching things turn around a little bit, gaining respect from certain people that I would never see it from," McKinney said. "Now that I see that they respect me, I respect them just as much. So it's very mutual."

He laughed while describing just how different those interactions are now.

"Now I can go out and have a normal conversation with somebody, and they don't just — I'm like, 'Hey,' and they just turn around and walk off," he said. "Now we can have a conversation like man to man, and it's pretty special to see where it was to where it is now."

In other words, he's not just the kid anymore.

"Exactly," McKinney said. "I feel more welcome. I feel like I'm out there having fun. We're doing our job. We're competing. We're competitors, and we realize that. But at the same time, we have the same respect as we do for everybody."

If there were any doubts left about whether McKinney belonged among the sport's best, he pretty well erased them on the St. Lawrence River.

RICKEY JACKSON WINS FIRST BASSMASTER RANDY MOSS PRO FOOTBALL HALL OF FAME PRO-AM ON ST. LAWRENCE RIVER

McKinney entered the final Elite Series event of the season with the Angler of the Year title within reach. He then caught a 30-pound, 11-ounce five-fish smallmouth limit on Day 2 — the heaviest in Bassmaster history — and put himself in position not only to win AOY but also to win the tournament.

By Sunday morning, however, the normally cool 21-year-old was feeling every ounce of what was at stake.

"I'd never been so nervous that it affected my fishing, really," McKinney said. "But no, it really did that last day."

There was a tournament win, $200,000 and the title he'd spent three years chasing all hanging on one final eight-hour day.

"I'd be lying if I said it didn't affect me because it did," he said. "I just didn't fish very good. I got nervous. I got impatient. I wanted it to be over quickly, and it just wasn't."

The fish weren't cooperating early, either.

McKinney hit his first few spots and came away with little to show for it. That's when the thoughts started creeping in.

"There's no way I've got all the way here. I've got a good pound cushion. I'm leading the tournament. There's no way I'm letting it slip through my hands. Not this time," he recalled thinking. "I added a lot of pressure to myself, I feel like, more than I should have."

That pressure was especially understandable considering how close he'd already come twice.

Strangely enough, those two previous runner-up finishes had actually helped him stay loose for most of the week.

"I was like, 'You know what? It is what it is. We've been here twice. What's going to happen? Get second again?'" McKinney said. "It kind of took the pressure off of us."

That worked until Sunday.

"All the work we have done literally has come down to this last eight hours, and that's where it all hit me," he said.

Eventually, McKinney landed a 6-pounder, and everything changed.

"Everything was good. Everything was all right, and we fished like normal Trey," he said.

McKinney ultimately finished second in the tournament, but it was more than enough to secure the Angler of the Year title.

And there was some poetic justice in who handed him the trophy.

Johnston, the man who had finished ahead of McKinney in the AOY race in each of the previous two seasons, was there to present it.

McKinney has plenty of respect for Johnston, whom he called an "unbelievable angler." He also admitted he enjoyed finally getting the better of him.

"He beat me fair and square. It is what it was," McKinney said. "But it did feel good to finally get one on him. Like, 'Hey, yeah, you've had the last two years. This one's mine.'"

With the win, McKinney broke a record that had stood since 1992, when Kevin VanDam became Bassmaster Angler of the Year at 24 years old.

McKinney said he didn't even realize until recently that he was still young enough to take that record from the man he called "pretty much the greatest of all time."

"It's pretty special," he said.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Safe to say, McKinney has earned his place.

At this point, nobody on the Elite Series should need much more convincing.

item.title: Lane Kiffin goes full villain mode during alleged halftime speech from LSU's blowout win over Clemson
item.description: Lane Kiffin's leaked halftime speech during LSU's 51-10 rout of Clemson shows college football's biggest villain fully embracing the hate.
item.content:encoded:
LSU sent a clear message, not only to Clemson, but to the entire country with its dominant first-half performance against the visiting Tigers in Week 1 by taking a 31-3 lead into the break. Thirty minutes of complete control was not enough for LSU head coach Lane Kiffin, however, not nearly enough, in fact.

With Kiffin's offseason bookended by a nasty exit from Ole Miss and court cases involving former NFL players potentially returning to college and suiting up for the Bayou Bengals, LSU and its newest head coach didn't exactly enter the season as 'America's Team.'

Someone has to claim the role of college football's biggest villain, and the most polarizing coach in the sport, leading a team that reportedly costs north of $40 million in NIL money and partnering with unsavory storylines galore.

TIME IS NOW, CLEMSON TIGERS AND DABO SWINNEY NEED TO CALL IT QUITS AFTER HISTORIC RUN

Through one game of the season, Kiffin and LSU aren't only thriving while playing the big bad villain, but fully embracing it.

Kiffin's alleged halftime speech from LSU's win over Clemson has leaked, and the message revealed a coach and a program fully leaning into the narrative that they're the most-hated in the sport.

LSU FANS BOO JAYDEN DANIELS DURING JUMBOTRON TRIBUTE AFTER NIL CEASE-AND-DESIST DISPUTE

"Alright, guys, we started here like seven, eight months ago, whatever it was," Kiffin said in the video. "We asked you to work really hard. We asked you to come back to work again and again and again. Do you feel good about what happened? Who gives a f— what happened? That’s what’s supposed to happen. There’s no f—ing celebrations for that. They’re f—ing soft.

"So you’ve got to show them again. They’re going to come out. It doesn’t matter what plays they run. It doesn’t matter what they do on offense, defense. Put the next motherf—ing quarterback in. I don’t give a f—. You send them a f–ing message who the f— is on their schedule. They have to play you.

"And don’t think we’re letting up late. No matter if you’re in the game for one more snap or 50 more snaps, you f—ing take it out on them. The whole f—ing world hates you. So you get a chance to show the whole world, ‘Go f— yourself.’ Clemson just had to see it right now."

Not only was LSU up 31-3 when Kiffin delivered the alleged speech, but the Tigers had held Clemson to just 54 total yards of offense on 25 plays and negative four yards on the ground.

Kiffin's message was delivered loud and clear, as LSU went on to outscore Clemson 20-7 in the second half to earn a 51-10 victory. LSU outgained Clemson by a stunning 499 yards on offense when it was all said and done.

item.title: 4 family members flying from Bahamas to Florida in small plane go missing, with Coast Guard joining search
item.description: Four Florida family members remain missing on Tuesday after their plane vanished while traveling home from the Bahamas over Labor Day weekend.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Coast Guard has joined the search for a plane carrying four Florida family members that authorities in the Bahamas believe "crash-landed" in the ocean after departing from Great Harbour Cay.

Pilot Mario Lamar, 80, his wife Lili, 79, and two of their grandchildren, Sofia Sosa, 28, and Christian Sosa, 22, were identified by family as those on board the PA-34 Piper five-seater aircraft that was heading to Opa-locka, Florida, according to the Miami Herald.

"Please help," Silvia Larrieu, the niece of the couple, told the newspaper. "I ask anybody out there, if you can help with search and rescue efforts, we would greatly appreciate it. We need to bring them home."

Larrieu said the four were coming home to Florida after visiting a vacation property in Great Harbour Cay over Labor Day weekend and that "they’ve spent their whole life going there." Data from the website FlightAware showed the plane descended from 10,000 feet to 3,700 feet in about three minutes before vanishing from radar.

AMAZON CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS MIAMI AIRPORT RUNWAY

Larrieu told the Miami Herald that Mario Lamar had years of experience as a pilot and always kept the aircraft in "pristine" shape.

U.S. Coast Guard Southeast said Monday it was assisting authorities in the Bahamas "following a report of a downed aircraft with four souls on board approx 15 mi off Andros Island," with a Coast Guard HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane joining the search.

The Royal Bahamas Police Force said it received a report around 2:20 p.m. on Monday "that an aircraft may have gone down in the waters off Red Bays."

COAST GUARD PLANE WITH DHS SECRETARY ONBOARD MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER ENGINE FAILURE

It added that air traffic control "confirmed that a PA-34 Piper five-seater aircraft, bearing tail number N212ML, departed Great Harbour Cay at approximately 11:12 a.m., en route to Opa-locka, Florida."

"Air traffic control subsequently lost contact with the aircraft approximately 13 miles west of Andros Island," the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.

"The Bahamas Air Sea Rescue Association (BASRA) advised that the United States Coast Guard had attempted to search the area for the missing aircraft," police also said. "However, due to inclement weather, the search was postponed until conditions became favorable."

item.title: Patriots lock up Christian Gonzalez as highest-paid NFL cornerback just before season opener at Seattle
item.description: Christian Gonzalez's $135 million Patriots extension makes him the NFL's highest-paid cornerback ever, but the deal's timing reveals a deeper trend.
item.content:encoded:
The headlines around NFL circles are blaring that Christian Gonzalez has become the highest-paid cornerback in the league's history and that is accurate and sounds consequential but it comes with a little secret:

Everyone expected this.

Gonzalez early Tuesday morning agreed to a four-year extension worth $135 million with the New England Patriots that includes $102 million in guaranteed money. Gonzalez confirmed the deal and its numbers on Instagram.

PATRICK MAHOMES LEAPS PAST DAK PRESCOTT AS NFL'S HIGHEST-PAID QB WITH RECORD CHIEFS EXTENSION WORTH $504.75M

The $33.75 million per season Gonzalez will get on an annual average basis not only makes him the highest-paid cornerback on average in the NFL, it makes him the league's highest-paid cornerback ever.

But this would have been bigger news if it had not happened.

TEXANS STAR DEFENDER BECOMES HIGHEST-PAID NON-QUARTERBACK IN NFL HISTORY WITH $150M DEAL: REPORTS

The reason this is a dog-bites-man story is every circumstance pointed to Gonzalez reaching this plateau and doing it exactly on this timing.

Why? Because NFL contracts for top players work a lot on three factors:

NFL salaries for top players rarely go down.

The NFL is about deadlines. It moves when deadlines loom. Gonzalez agreed to his deal less than 48 hours before the start of the regular season, with the Patriots leaving Tuesday for the NFL's regular-season opener at Seattle on Wednesday evening.

The Patriots and Gonzalez simply made certain both started the season on the right footing rather than embroiled in contract strife. It would have been a bad look for everyone if this had not happened by the opener, so obviously the timing of the approaching season moved things forward.

The market for this deal was set this offseason when Los Angeles Rams cornerback Trent McDuffie agreed to his new deal in March, then Cleveland Browns cornerback Denzel Ward agreed to a deal in late July, then Seattle Seahawks cornerback Devon Witherspoon agreed to his new deal in mid-August.

While those negotiations were reaching their expected end, the Patriots clearly knew the assignment they faced.

"We love Christian Gonzalez," Patriots owner Robert Kraft said during training camp. "We love him as a player and as a person. That's why we've made an offer to him that makes him the highest-paid player ever to play that position in the NFL, and, coincidentally, it's the highest contract in Patriots' franchise history."

That offer on the table in late July needed adjusting because the price of paying a cornerback more than anyone else at the position kept climbing. 

McDuffie got a deal that averages $31 million per season.

Ward got a deal that averages $31.1 million per season.

Witherspoon got a deal that averages $33 million per season.

So, now Gonzalez, the latest of the best cornerbacks to sign, gets a deal worth $33.75 million per season.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

See how that works?

The league's best players get raises and when they're scheduled for new contracts and those come at higher plateaus than the last star at the same position because both teams and agents want to show they did right by their players.

And Gonzalez, 24, is the right guy.

He was drafted No. 17 overall in the 2023 draft. He was a second-team AP All-Pro in 2024 and a Pro Bowler in 2025. He had 10 passes defensed in 14 regular-season games last year. He also had seven passes defensed, a forced fumble, and an interception in New England’s four 2025 postseason games.

He's arguably the NFL's best cornerback.

And his perfect timing and the machinery that affects league salaries made him its highest-paid cornerback.

item.title: US rebuilding weapons stockpile could delay orders from allies
item.description: Patriot missile stockpiles have dropped to 36% of pre-Iran war levels as allies face delayed deliveries and U.S. rebuilds its defense inventory.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. has for years been the top weapons supplier in the world. Over the past five years, arms exports have gone to nearly 100 countries.

"These weapons are sought after around the world because we have the best weapons," said War Department Under Secretary for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey.

The Trump administration says some of the U.S. stockpile depletion is because of the weapons given to Ukraine. The Center for Strategic and International Studies assesses those transfers have been a minor factor in the shrinking U.S. inventories except for one important tool – the Patriot Missile Defense System.

WEAPONS STOCKPILE SHORTAGES IMPACTING MILITARY STRATEGY IN THE MIDEAST

"We've maxed out the production lines now, and that process began during the Ukraine War when it was clear that modern conflict was going to require a lot more munitions than we had been planning on," said Mark Cancian, a retired U.S. Marine colonel and senior advisor with the CSIS Defense and Security Department.

Between 2021 and 2025, Ukraine was the largest recipient of major arms around the world, with at least 36 countries supplying weapons. The U.S. was the top supplier over the five-year time period, accounting for 41% of Ukrainian arms imports.

AS CHINA TENSIONS LOOM, US TEMPORARILY PAUSES TAIWAN WEAPONS SALES DUE TO IRAN WAR, ACTING NAVY SECRETARY SAYS

Before Russia’s war in Ukraine began in 2022, CSIS estimates the U.S. had around 2,200 Patriot missiles in its inventory. Estimates show around 600 missiles were given to Ukraine, with a few of those possibly coming from U.S. allies. Deliveries of new production outpaced the number given to Ukraine, with an estimated 2,300 missiles in the U.S. Patriot inventory before the Iran conflict began. It’s estimated that around 36% of Patriot Interceptors remain from the pre-Iran war inventory.

"As chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee, my job is to sign off on all foreign military weapons and sales to countries like Israel, to countries, like Taiwan and Ukraine, for that matter. And when we can't deliver on that promise because we can't make those weapons fast enough, it hurts our alliances, it hurts allies' ability to protect themselves," said Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas.

Publicly available government reports show at least four countries, including the U.S., have provided full Patriot missile systems to Ukraine. The U.S. is the only country that manufactures the Patriot battery, and one of two countries, along with Japan, to publicly show it produces Patriot missiles.

"If we take all of the Patriots for ourselves, and of course, that's 600 a year, we can refill the inventory much more quickly, but we have frozen out our allies and partners," Cancian said.

UKRAINE SEEKS MORE US PATRIOT INTERCEPTORS AS BOMB SHELTER PROBE DEEPENS

Patriot producer Raytheon says, "Patriot is the foundation of integrated air and missile defense for 19 nations." But as the U.S. prioritizes rebuilding its weapons inventory, deliveries for some countries are already delayed.

"Unfortunately, the world we live in is an increasing threat, and that means that we need a bigger military force, and we need a stronger defense industrial base to be able to equip the warfighter and supply all that we need to win the fight," Duffey said.

Patriot batteries and Tomahawk missiles were first used in Operation Desert Storm. At least two other countries have Tomahawks and while the stockpile remains large compared to other systems, at around two-thirds of its prewar inventory, new orders from Japan and the Netherlands could face delays.

"With Tomahawk, we have the same situation with the Japanese. They bought 400. They're told they're being pushed back in the queue. On the other hand, they're facing China. They've reconfigured one of their ships to take the Tomahawks. So, there's again going to be a diplomatic discussion there," Cancian said.

MORE THAN HALF OF SOME US WEAPONS STOCKPILES USED IN IRAN WAR, RAISING CONCERNS ABOUT CHINA THREAT

Just the U.S., the UAE and Saudi Arabia have THAAD systems. Their first confirmed use was in 2022 after a UAE system intercepted missiles launched by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. No official delays have been reported for THAAD orders, but the U.S. has 52%-62% of its inventory remaining and outstanding deliveries for Saudi Arabia, expected to be completed by April 2028.

"This military competition we're in with China and Russia and Iran is real. And we have to win that competition," McCaul said.

OPINION: AMERICA FACES A CRISIS IN OUR MILITARY ARSENAL THAT TRUMP IS RACING TO FIX

The ground-launched Precision Strike Missile (PrSm), developed by Lockheed Martin, was first used in Operation Epic Fury. CSIS says just 10-22% of those weapons remain from pre-Iran conflict levels, following the ceasefire expenditures and revised estimates from the beginning of the conflict in late February.

"It's important to keep in mind that the level of intensity in those 14 days of renewed conflict were not as high as they were during the first 39 days of the air war," Cancian said about the July strikes after the ceasefire ended. "During the 14 days, the U.S. was launching maybe 80 to 100 strikes according to the Pentagon per day. During the 39 days of the major air war, we were launching about 350 strikes a day, plus Israel was launching another 200 to 250. So, the intensity wasn't quite as high, but we were still going through these munitions."

item.title: Divers uncover hundreds of ancient relics near shipwreck untouched for 2,100 years
item.description: Pictures show hundreds of intact amphorae scattered across the seabed near Mazara del Vallo, where a Roman shipwreck lay hidden for over 2,000 years.
item.content:encoded:
Archaeologists recently uncovered a roughly 2,100-year-old shipwreck off the coast of Sicily — along with hundreds of remnants of its ancient cargo.

The discovery was announced last month by the Italian Ministry of Culture. The ruins are about three miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo, a city located about 50 miles southwest of Palermo.

The wreck was discovered during a joint inspection by Italian cultural heritage officials and Carabinieri diving units after private citizens reported the site.

MYSTERY OF GOLD COIN SHIPWRECK FINALLY UNMASKED AFTER 30 YEARS: 'FANTASTIC CONCLUSION'

The Roman-era wreck dates between the second and first centuries B.C., the ministry said.

Divers found the site at a depth of about 150 feet.

"Hundreds of amphorae, predominantly of the Dressel 1A type, are present on the seabed, along with two lead anchor stocks and another structure made of the same material," officials said in a translated statement.

Pictures show hundreds of ancient amphorae clustered across the seabed, many still remarkably intact despite spending more than 2,000 years underwater.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Amphorae, ceramic vessels commonly used throughout the ancient world, were often used to carry wine and olive oil, though officials have not said what the vessels found aboard the wreck once contained.

In a statement, Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli called the find "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years."

He added, "The sea continues to return precious fragments of our history to us, and the Mazara del Vallo shipwreck tells us about the people, routes and trade that made the Mediterranean a crossroads of civilizations."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Research will continue to uncover its history and make it available to the public."

Sicily's Superintendency of the Sea will conduct further research to learn more about the site's history and establish measures to protect it.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The Mediterranean Sea, a hub of maritime trade for thousands of years, is filled with ancient shipwrecks that continue to yield new discoveries.

Earlier this summer, archaeologists announced the discovery of gold jewelry aboard a roughly 1,300-year-old shipwreck off a Croatian island.

Last summer, divers exploring another ancient wreck off the coast of Turkey uncovered hundreds of well-preserved ceramics dating back roughly 2,000 years.

item.title: Massive fire engulfs apartment complex under construction, forces evacuations in South Bend
item.description: A massive construction fire engulfed the Stadium Flats apartments in South Bend, Indiana, forcing emergency evacuation of neighboring residents.
item.content:encoded:
A massive fire early Tuesday morning tore through an apartment complex under construction in South Bend, Indiana, forcing residents of a neighboring building to evacuate, according to local officials.

The South Bend Fire Department said the fire began just after midnight at the Stadium Flats apartments near S. Lafayette & W. South Street.

Fire crews arrived to a scene of towering flames and billowing smoke after receiving reports that the blaze had engulfed both the building under construction and a crane.

CRANE ARM COLLAPSES INTO MIAMI CONDO ROOFTOP POOL AREA AS WORKERS CLING TO DANGLING STRUCTURE

Despite the fire producing "a significant amount of embers and debris," firefighters were able to keep it from spreading to the neighboring Diamond View Apartments.

Residents of the Diamond View Apartments were evacuated during the fire, with officials saying the heat damaged several windows on the building's top floor. The building has 60 units of affordable housing, according to a report last year in the South Bend Tribune.

MASSIVE CHEMICAL FIRE ERUPTS AT ELECTRICAL TRANSFORMER PLANT IN MISSISSIPPI, FORCING EVACUATION

The Stadium Flats building was set to introduce 92 additional affordable units to downtown South Bend. Before the fire, construction was expected to be completed by spring 2027.

Both buildings are near the training facility for the South Bend Cubs, the city's minor league baseball team. Firefighters were able to stop the blaze from spreading to the 17,000-square-foot complex, which is right next to the baseball stadium.

Officials said the cause of the fire remains under investigation. No injuries or deaths were reported.

The fire occurred a little over two miles from the University of Notre Dame's campus.

item.title: Art heist thieves make off with Renoir paintings worth millions from museum on French Riviera
item.description: Two thieves cut through a fence at the French Riviera's Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, stealing four paintings but dropping two as police closed in.
item.content:encoded:
Thieves made off with two valuable Renoir paintings after breaking into a small museum on the French Riviera early Tuesday, dropping two other stolen works in the garden as police raced to the scene, officials said.

The two thieves cut through a garden fence and entered the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer shortly before 6 a.m., stealing four paintings, Mayor Bryan Masson said.

The alarm sounded at 5:48 a.m. Police arrived five minutes later and chased the thieves, who dropped two of the paintings in the garden before escaping with the other two, according to Masson.

NJ FATHER-DAUGHTER TEAM ACCUSED OF PEDDLING FAKE PICASSOS, WARHOLS AND MORE TO NYC ART HOUSES PLEAD GUILTY

"Attacking the Renoir Museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer," Masson said, further calling for tighter security at museums across France.

Surveillance cameras captured two people entering the museum. Police were still looking for them Tuesday.

The four paintings taken included "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano," "Coco Lisant" and "Young Girl at the Well," according to French newspaper Nice-Matin, which valued the stolen works at about $10.5 million.

A regional police official confirmed the theft and search for the suspects to The Associated Press but could not confirm the reported value. It was also unclear which two paintings the thieves abandoned as they fled.

The museum remained closed Tuesday while police investigated.

The Renoir Museum is housed in the hilltop estate where French Impressionist Pierre-Auguste Renoir spent the final years of his life and died in 1919.

WATCH: MASKED THIEVES WIELDING HAMMERS HIT JEWELRY STORE IN WHAT EXPERT CALLS 'MOB-STYLE' HEIST

The museum, which opened in 1960, sits in Cagnes-sur-Mer between Nice and Cannes on France’s Mediterranean coast. Its collection includes 13 Renoir paintings, about 40 sculptures, furniture and photographs.

Tuesday’s theft follows a series of museum robberies in France, including last year’s theft of crown jewels from the Louvre in Paris.

Thieves stole jewels valued at about $102 million from the Louvre in October, including a tiara that belonged to Empress Eugénie.

Europol said last month that art robberies in Europe have grown more violent and that some thefts once carried out by specialist gangs are now being committed by opportunists recruited through social media.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

item.title: 105-year-old credits ‘the good Lord’ for her long life: ‘Every day is a blessing’
item.description: Blynda Vidock of Baytown, Texas, still lives independently at 105 and credits faith, athletics and eating well for her remarkable longevity.
item.content:encoded:
A Texas woman who just turned 105 attributes her long life to "the good Lord." 

While Blynda Vidock's faith may have played an important role in her longevity, the Baytown resident has also followed many of the habits that experts say can contribute to a longer, healthier life.

"The good Lord put me here for so many years, and it’s His life through me," she told FOX 26 Houston at her recent birthday celebration. "But I’ve always been very athletic, played tennis, swam all my life and ate good food."

GEORGIA WOMAN CELEBRATES 112TH BIRTHDAY, REVEALS HER SECRET TO A LONG LIFE

Vidock joked that she preaches to her children, grandchildren and "great-grands" to eat healthier, but said, "They still eat junk food!"

"We live faster nowadays," she said. "We used to have time to sit down and have a meal together."

Vidock was born in 1921 and grew up in West Palm Beach, Florida. While working for $15 a week at a bank in West Palm Beach, she crossed paths with big-name movie stars Clark Gable and Fred Astaire, and also recalled encountering a young John F. Kennedy.

She met Coast Guardsman Charles "Chuck" Vidock while volunteering with the USO during World War II. The two married and moved to Texas in 1946 and spent decades traveling the world together.

LONGEVITY DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR AGING WELL, BEYOND PRICEY BIOHACKS

Vidock is "completely sharp, independent and full of stories from a century of living," according to the report.

A video from her birthday party shows the centenarian walking around and chatting animatedly with the many friends and family members who gathered to honor her.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"It’s wonderful to have you people here, and I don’t know if I’m supposed to dance or sing or get up on the table," she said. "I think I've been made queen for a day, and I've got my 15 minutes of fame, so you better enjoy it because it won't come again."

Every morning when she wakes up, Vidock said she wonders, "‘This is another day, Lord, why am I here?’" adding, "Every day is a blessing!"

She said "the saddest part about getting old" is watching people lose their mental sharpness and credits "the good Lord" with allowing her to keep hers.

Vidock said a few simple habits have helped her live so long.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Living like you know you’re supposed to live, being kind to people, and everything in moderation helped, and I got blessed with good genes, but then I took care of my body," she said.

Dr. Annu Navani, chief medical officer at Le Reve Wellness in San Jose, California, recently told Fox News Digital that longevity medicine is more about adding life to years than adding years to life.

Rather than splurging on costly biohacks, procedures or supplements, Navani recommends focusing on simple daily practices that can enhance quality of life.

Getting high-quality sleep — about seven hours a night for the average person — is necessary for people to perform optimally and has been linked to a healthier lifespan, the expert said.

Managing stress is another key factor in healthy aging, according to Navani. Regular physical activity and social interaction — two other factors linked to longevity — can also help people keep stress in check, as can regular meditation.

Eating a nutritious diet that includes a variety of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, protein and dairy, while limiting added sugars and ultraprocessed foods, is another important component of healthy aging.

Longevity experts David Cravit and Larry Wolf, authors of "The SuperAging Workbook," previously told Fox News Digital that maintaining a positive attitude is the No. 1 factor linked to living a longer life.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"People with a positive attitude outlive people with a negative attitude because it reduces stress, which, in turn, reduces inflammation, and inflammation is the cause of most age-related diseases," Cravit said.

The authors also recommended setting and working toward new goals, building strong relationships and maintaining a sense of independence as people age.

Melissa Rudy and Angelica Stabile of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

item.title: Prince Harry finds way to live ‘half-in, half-out’ life Queen Elizabeth refused to endorse: experts
item.description: Prince Harry and Meghan's U.K. return with their children echoes the "half-in, half-out" proposal Queen Elizabeth II rejected at Sandringham.
item.content:encoded:
Prince Harry may have finally found a way to live the life that his grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, refused to endorse.

On Sept. 8, 2022, Britain's longest-reigning monarch died after 70 years on the throne. She was 96. On Aug. 26 this year, Harry and his wife, Meghan Markle, returned to the U.K., where their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, will attend school.

As the Sussexes settle into their new life in Britain, with details about their private home and their children's school closely guarded, royal experts told Fox News Digital that the arrangement recalls the "half-in, half-out" proposal the late queen rejected.

PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK MOVE PUTS FRESH SPOTLIGHT ON THEIR EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS AGAINST ROYAL FAMILY

"Harry may feel vindicated because, superficially, he has created something resembling the freedom he originally wanted," Kinsey Schofield, host of the YouTube show "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. "But I think calling it a victory misunderstands what the queen rejected."

"I see absolutely no reason to believe she would have changed her mind," Schofield said. "Queen Elizabeth spent 70 years protecting the distinction between the crown and the individual. It seems unlikely that one of the defining judgements of her final years would suddenly have become negotiable."

While the Sussexes have returned to the U.K. for an extended stay, they won't resume their roles as working royals. They will live in a private, non-royal residence outside London while maintaining their California home and a property in Portugal. People magazine reported that Meghan is in early talks for a role in the Netflix drama "The Gentlemen."

WATCH: PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE CAUSED QUEEN STRESS IN FINAL YEARS: AUTHOR

On Monday, the Lord Chamberlain, the most senior official in the royal household, sent a letter to senior officials in the government and military, as well as lord lieutenants, the king's personal representatives around the country.

The letter drew a firm line around the Sussexes’ homecoming, reaffirming that the couple will not resume official duties. 

"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of The Sovereign, and are no longer working Members of The Royal Family," a letter sent on behalf of King Charles III read, Fox News can confirm. "This position, distinct from the State and Royal duties undertaken by the working Royal Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected."

"It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex," the letter added. "Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and are not used. The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity. In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests."

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals in 2020 after describing intense scrutiny from the British press and saying they lacked support from the palace.

"Following conversations with the duke, the queen has written confirming that in stepping away from the work of the royal family it is not possible to continue with the responsibilities and duties that come with a life of public service," a statement from Buckingham Palace read at the time.

In response, the couple issued a statement of their own, saying: "We can all live a life of service. Service is universal."

British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital the queen drew a firm line before the couple's departure, insisting the Sussexes could not be "half in, half out" as working royals.

"Her position was simply stated as ‘all in or all out,’" Fordwich said. "While King Charles has maintained that position, he is likely to be more open to private reconciliation and family gatherings, especially if Harry refrains from further public attacks on the family. Prince William, however, remains resistant to any formal restoration of royal duties for Harry."

In 2020, Harry attended the Sandringham Summit at Queen Elizabeth II's Norfolk estate, where senior royals determined the terms of his and Meghan's departure from royal life.

According to People magazine, it was there that the late queen made her position clear. After lengthy discussions, Harry was told there would be no "half-in, half-out" role for the Sussexes. They could not remain working royals while also pursuing independent, income-generating ventures.

In his memoir "Spare," Harry recalled the Sandringham meeting and wrote that he believed the royals would consider five options for the Sussexes. "Option Five" called for a full departure. After about an hour, the queen's private secretary — nicknamed "The Bee" by Harry — distributed drafts of a statement announcing "Option Five." Harry wrote that he was stunned.

"Wait. I'm confused," he wrote. "You've already drafted a statement? Before any discussion? Announcing Option Five? In other words, the fix was in this whole time? This summit was just for show?"

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital he believes the palace made a mistake by rejecting the proposal outright.

"In my view, the queen was very badly advised by her representatives over the ‘half in, half out’ policy," he said. "I cannot see any reason in this day and age why it could not work. It shows a level of hypocrisy. Harry and Meghan could have remained in the royal fold without costs to the public purse. And yet, this was deemed unacceptable."

Schofield argued the queen had good reason to reject the proposal.

"The queen had already learned the dangers of ‘half in, half out’ long before Harry and Meghan proposed it," she explained.

"Prince Edward and Duchess Sophie attempted to maintain commercial careers alongside royal duties, with Edward running his television company and Sophie working in public relations. The arrangement became increasingly uncomfortable for the institution, especially as their professional lives generated headlines that risked trading on their royal connections. Ultimately, they abandoned those careers and became full-time working royals."

"That experience demonstrated exactly why the lines need to be clear," Schofield continued. "You are either representing the Crown and accepting the restrictions that come with that privilege, or you are pursuing a private, commercial life. Trying to do both inevitably raises questions about royal status, access and whether relationships are being leveraged for personal gain."

Schofield argued senior royals dedicate themselves fully to serving the crown and supporting the monarch as a united front. She said it would have been "unfair" to relax those restrictions for the Sussexes while allowing them to benefit from their royal status. In the queen's eyes, commercial freedom was "incompatible" with royal service.

"The queen might have wanted more family connection with Harry and Meghan, but she wouldn’t have compromised the constitutional aspects of such an arrangement," Fordwich said. "She would also have been deeply wary of the commercial conflicts it could create. It would have set a precedent for other royals wanting to have it both ways."

Before Harry and Meghan returned to Britain, Simon Vigar, author of "The Four Wives of Windsor," told Fox News Digital that a "hybrid" model was inevitable.

"[The Sussexes] thought they could have a hybrid role of having a business life and a private life, while also spending a few months in the U.K. supporting the queen," he shared. "Harry believed that was an option, which was whipped away from him."

WATCH: PRINCE HARRY BELIEVED ROYAL FAMILY COULD HAVE ALLOWED A ‘HYBRID’ ROLE: AUTHOR

After stepping back from royal duties, the Sussexes signed lucrative deals with Netflix and Spotify and publicly aired their grievances in interviews, documentaries and Harry's memoir, further straining his relationship with the royal family.

In 2025, Harry told the BBC he was ready for reconciliation and eager to spend more time with his father, who is being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer.

According to a source close to the Sussexes, Meghan will continue leading her As Ever company from the U.K., while Harry will spend more time working with his U.K.-based charities.

In July, the Sussexes privately met with the king at his Highgrove estate. It was the first time Archie and Lilibet had seen their grandfather since the late queen’s Platinum Jubilee in 2022.

Schofield questioned whether Harry has any regrets about his grandmother's final years.

"Harry says he loved his grandmother, and has spoken very warmly about their relationship," she said.

"But some of his choices during her final years became part of an already difficult period for the royal family. Whatever grievances Harry had with the institution, his grandmother was elderly, recently widowed and approaching the end of an entire life of service. There are conversations he can never have with her and decisions he can never revisit with her."

item.title: Twenty-Five years later, Hollywood is giving 9/11 the silent treatment, and it’s making us less safe
item.description: The absence of September 11 films left a vacuum filled by conspiracy theorists, while filmmakers rallied for Gaza instead of grappling with terrorism.
item.content:encoded:
I am a historian, but you don’t need a PhD to realize that Americans and Brits learn most of what we know about the world from the movies.

When most people think about World War II, for example, we think about the first few minutes of Stephen Spielberg’s Saving Private Ryan, or this summer, we are discovering the critical role of the chief Allied meteorologist, Captain James Stagg, through the new film, Pressure. We learned all about Vietnam from Apocalypse Now, Full Metal Jacket and Platoon. And Glory did more to make the Civil War feel accessible and immediate than even the best histories on that seminal conflict.

Which is why it’s not only dispiriting but, frankly, deeply concerning that even now, a quarter of a century later, we’ve had so few movies about the attacks of September 11, 2001.

9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS

True, Oliver Stone gave us World Trade Center, and Paul Greengrass United 93, both celebrations of ordinary Americans making extraordinary sacrifices on that fateful day. But other than these two dramas and a handful of notable documentaries, the great cultural machine that, for nearly a century, had told us the stories we needed to hear to make sense of ourselves and the world went largely silent. In fact, the last feature film on 9/11 was made over a decade ago, with none currently in the pipeline.

Why?

It’s a fascinating question, one that’s likely to keep future historians busy.

You can blame it on progressive sensibilities, a DEI mindset, and not wanting to risk being accused of Islamophobia by producing movies that make Muslims look like the bad guys.

DEAN CAIN SAYS HOLLYWOOD'S WOKE ERA IS ENDING: 'WE'LL LOOK BACK AND SAY THAT WAS STUPID'

You can blame it on post-modernism, which favors irony and metaphor over direct engagement with difficult topics. When asked why he’d never made a movie about 9/11, for example, Spielberg replied that he had: 2005’s War of the Worlds, which features many scenes of urban devastation, but which does very little to help us think seriously about one of the most challenging moments in American history.

You can blame it on the way movies are financed these days, with money coming in from investors all over the world, including from countries that aren’t really interested in heralding the values of the West.

But whatever the reason, the bottom line remains the same: By failing to make movies that grapple with the reasons for and the responses to 9/11, Hollywood has made America and its allies weaker, more vulnerable and less safe.

How so? Let us count the ways.

US ARMY HITS 2026 RECRUITING GOALS FOUR MONTHS EARLY, PETE HEGSETH ANNOUNCES AT WEST POINT COMMENCEMENT

First, look at the rates of enlistment to the U.S. armed forces. In 1986, for example, Navy recruiters saw a whopping 500% spike in young people eager to enlist — they had all watched Top Gun and left the theater thinking that naval service was not just worthy but desirable. Enlistment numbers remained solid throughout the 1990s and immediately after 9/11, but the early 2000s showed a drastic decline with the recruiting crisis reaching its peak in 2022-23.

Hollywood’s failures, however, run even deeper.

No serious person, patriotic as they may be, could argue that Hollywood has any obligation to reflect this ideology or that. But most serious people should argue that filmmakers are artists, and as such are at their finest when they grapple with the most pressing eras of their time. We consider Casablancaa classic, for example, in large part because it was filmed and released in the middle of World War II, giving us unforgettable characters that resonated with us precisely because they were forced to ask themselves who we were fighting and why.

And when artists stop asking these questions seriously, moral confusion ensues.

AS AMERICAN PRIDE HITS A 25-YEAR LOW, A NEW 9/11 EDUCATION PLATFORM URGES THE NATION TO NEVER FORGET

We knew the Nazis were bad because we had decades of movies exploring their wickedness. And even if we couldn’t agree on the scope of American military engagement in Southeast Asia, no serious Hollywood filmmaker thought it wise to glorify the Vietcong or their supporters. The result was a culture that could have robust disagreements about important questions without losing track of the fact that America was a benevolent nation doing its best to safeguard freedom, democracy, and the other virtues of Western civilization.

When Hollywood went silent and stopped making thoughtful movies about our wars, it created a huge cultural vacuum. And because nature abhors a vacuum — life, as a famous Hollywood movie once put it, always finds a way — that vacuum was filled by conspiracy theories. Crackpots like Alex Jones and Candace Owens and Tucker Carlson can only thrive because people need stories to help them make sense of the world, and if serious filmmakers won’t tell them, then the lunatics sure will.

If that wasn’t bad enough, the same filmmakers who had so shamefully failed to wrestle with our recent history added insult to injury by showing up en masse, in the aftermath of Oct. 7, 2023, to advocate not for America and its challenges but for Gaza, currently governed by a terror group that shares an ideology with the Jihadis who attacked us 25 years ago this month.

This is all very depressing. But if you’ve watched even a handful of good, old-fashioned Hollywood movies, you know that a setback in act II almost always becomes an opportunity in act III. The same technology that gave us AI slop can also be used to tell more ambitious stories more cheaply.

All we need now is a hero, some enterprising young director who could look back to that grim day in September and deliver an informative and inspiring film. And if Hollywood had taught us anything, it’s that heroes are never in short supply in America.

item.title: Unearthed interview exposes what Talarico thought about 'tough-on-crime' tactics
item.description: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico pushed restorative justice over suspension and expulsion, linking school discipline to criminal reform.
item.content:encoded:
James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, once framed disciplinary practices in schools as an outflow of the ideas behind criminal justice reforms he hoped lawmakers would implement in Texas.

"I’m recently excited about the formation of a bipartisan criminal justice reform caucus in the Texas House with prominent Democrats and prominent Republicans who understand that we have to move away from a tough-on-crime approach to a smart-on-crime approach, and that, I think, filters down to our schools," Talarico said in a 2020 interview on school disciplinary practices and their effect on minorities.

Talarico’s train of thought, from criminal reform laws to changes in educational discipline, demonstrates his underlying beliefs about moving away from punitive corrections.

SOROS NETWORK REBUILDS PROGRESSIVE PROSECUTOR PUSH AFTER STRING OF ELECTION LOSSES

Talarico fleshed out his view, detailing how the changes would affect the educational system.

"[We are] starting in elementary school, where we really pursue restorative practices that are going to rehabilitate our students who are suffering from trauma, our students who are feeling unsafe in school and our students who harm a classroom community."

Talarico was referring to "restorative justice," a view that links misbehavior to past personal and emotional experiences. In the words of Texas Appleseed, a group that promotes "social, economic and racial justice," restorative justice in education emphasizes the relational cost of conflict as a way to deter future bad behavior. "Restorative Justice, when applied to a school setting, focuses on how student behavior has harmed others and how to make amends. Schools use it to build community and strengthen student–school connections," the group wrote in a definition submitted to lawmakers.

The approach is often mentioned as an alternative to "zero tolerance" policies that focus on punishments that deter discouraged conduct.

To Talarico, its adoption could deemphasize other forms of punishments.

"What that means is really allowing students to repair the harms that they’ve caused in a classroom community. It's a lot more rigorous and a lot more effective than just expelling a student or suspending a student or removing them from a classroom community," Talarico said.

While in the Texas legislature in 2021, Talarico introduced a bill, HB 62, which would have sought to move schools away from in-school suspension, out-of-school suspension and removing kids to alternative educational programs.

The bill stalled in committee and never became law.

NORTH CAROLINA TEACHER'S KILLING REIGNITES SCRUTINY OF ROY COOPER'S CRIMINAL JUSTICE RECORD IN SENATE RACE

In the wake of the Uvalde school shooting in 2022, Republican lawmakers pushed back against Talarico’s line of reasoning, arguing that, despite some calls for leniency, repercussions for problematic behavior are sometimes unavoidable.

"Look, I don't want to see a kid go to jail for being caught with some pot. I don't want to see a kid go to jail because he gets into a fight with another kid," Texas state Rep. Steve Toth, a Republican, told interviewers.

"That's clearly not the intent here. But if you've got a kid that is violent and is consistently violent, and they've been violent toward other children and teachers, then we either have to reach that kid or we have to remove that kid. They shouldn't be in the classroom. Period."

Talarico’s statements are consistent with past calls to step away from law enforcement and prisons and towards social programs — calls that also show his beliefs about the best ways to deter criminal behavior.

"If we took just half of what we spent on wars, prisons, and policing and spent it on education, health care, and jobs, we could make prisons obsolete," Talarico said in a 2022 speech to a graduation ceremony for incarcerated students.

A little later on in that same speech, Talarico went further, calling the idea of prisons themselves a kind of violence.

"My experience as a teacher, a legislator, and a Christian tells me that birds don’t belong in cages; children don’t belong in cages; people don’t belong in cages. Poverty is violence. Pollution is violence. And yes, prison is violence," Talarico said.

MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED FIRES BACK AT CNN CHOOSING TO 'FIXATE' ON 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS

"I’m not asking you to join the system; I’m asking you to change the system. Dismantle this system of violence."

When asked about his views on criminal justice and how they link to education, Talarico's campaign said he has always prioritized both safety and smart-on-crime approaches, noting that he had been a member of the state's criminal reform caucus.

"James joined his Republican colleagues on this caucus because as a former public school teacher, James cares about keeping Texas students safe. James agrees with most Texans that we government should be smart-on-crime, and our students deserve all the support possible," JT Ennis, a campaign spokesperson, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"While James has passed bills in the legislature to deny bail for violent criminals, crack down on violent felons and send billions of dollars to support law enforcement, Ken Paxton has abused his office to benefit his wealthy donors and the well-connected — allowing criminals back on the street even as it made Texans less safe. Even Ken Paxton’s fellow Republicans have blasted his public safety record: more murders, soft on human trafficking, and pedophiles walking free," he added, referring to Talarico's Republican challenger, former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Having cleared the primary and secured his party's nomination, Talarico will face off against Paxton in the Nov. 3 general election.

item.title: How to stream safely while traveling outside the US
item.description: A VPN encrypts your connection on hotel, airport and café Wi-Fi abroad, but streaming catalogs and live sports access still depend on provider rules.
item.content:encoded:
Traveling abroad used to mean leaving your normal entertainment routine at home. Now, your streaming subscriptions can come with you. However, hotels, airports and cafés often mean unfamiliar Wi-Fi networks and different streaming catalogs.

If you want to stream safely while traveling outside the U.S., a VPN, or virtual private network, can help. It creates an encrypted connection between your device and the VPN server. That adds useful protection when you are on a network you do not control.

A VPN can also let you choose a server in your home country. That can be useful when you sign in to streaming services you already use. Still, content availability depends on the service, your subscription and local licensing rules. Here's what to know before you travel so you can protect your connection, stream more smoothly and avoid surprises along the way.

INSTANTLY UPGRADE YOUR STREAMING: AT HOME AND WHEN TRAVELING

Free Wi-Fi makes travel easier. Yet you often do not know who runs the network, how it is configured or who else is connected. Most major websites and apps already use HTTPS encryption. Even so, a VPN adds another encrypted tunnel between your device and the VPN server. That can reduce what the local network can learn about your internet activity.

This protection is useful beyond streaming. You may check email, book a reservation or sign in to an account while you are away. Turning on a VPN before using unfamiliar Wi-Fi adds another layer of privacy. Of course, a VPN does not make every public network risk-free. You should still avoid suspicious Wi-Fi names, keep your devices updated and use strong account security.

Streaming can get more complicated when you cross international borders. A service may offer one catalog in the U.S. and another in Europe or Australia. Licensing agreements, regional rights and company policies often determine what appears. A VPN can be useful here because it gives you a secure way to connect to the internet while you sign in to subscriptions you normally use at home. You can also choose a VPN server in the U.S. when you need a U.S.-based connection.

However, a VPN does not guarantee access to a particular show, movie, channel or sporting event. Streaming companies set their own terms of use and regional availability rules. A program you watch at home may therefore be unavailable at your destination. Before you travel, check your streaming provider's current policies and the availability of anything you especially want to watch.

If you want a secure U.S. connection while traveling, set everything up before you leave. That way, you are not troubleshooting from an airport lounge or hotel room.

Choose a reputable VPN service and create your account before your trip. Look for one that offers U.S. server locations, apps for the devices you use and enough simultaneous connections for the people traveling with you.

Install the VPN app on every phone, tablet or computer you plan to bring. Then, sign in and test the connection before you leave home. This also gives you time to solve any password, installation or account problems while you still have a reliable connection.

Open your VPN and choose a U.S. server location. Once connected, open your streaming service and sign in normally. Websites and streaming services see the VPN server's IP address instead of your usual public IP address, while the connection between your device and the VPN server remains encrypted. Your streaming provider still decides what programming your account can access.

TRAVEL MISTAKE PUTS PHONE, LAPTOP AND STREAMING ACCOUNTS AT RISK

Streaming services have their own rules for VPN connections, regional access and travel. Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video, YouTube, ESPN and Apple TV+ may handle VPN connections differently, so check your service before you travel.

The exact shows, movies, channels and sporting events you can watch also depend on your subscription and the streaming provider's regional rules.

That is especially important for live TV and sports. Broadcast rights can change by country, league and even individual event. If there is something specific you want to watch during your trip, check the service before you leave.

A VPN can also protect your connection while you watch live sports through subscriptions you already have. That can be useful for football, basketball, baseball, hockey, tennis, cycling, golf and other events when you are away from home.

However, a VPN does not create a subscription or eliminate a provider's blackout rules. Your streaming service still controls access based on your plan, location and its current broadcasting agreements. For that reason, check the event and service before relying on it for a big game.

The best time to prepare is before you are standing in an airport with spotty Wi-Fi. Download the VPN app on your phone, tablet or laptop. Sign in and test it. Also, update your streaming apps before departure.

Next, sign in to the services you expect to use. Some platforms may ask you to verify your identity when they detect a new device or location. Handling that at home can save time later. If your service supports offline viewing, download a few shows or movies before you go. Offline downloads are especially useful on planes, trains and trips where the connection may be unreliable.

When you use a VPN, your traffic travels through the VPN server before reaching the internet. Distance can affect performance. If you mainly want extra privacy and do not need a particular country, choose a nearby server. A shorter distance can often improve speed and latency.

If you need a U.S. IP address for a service you normally use at home, connect to a U.S. server instead. If the stream slows down, try another server in the same country. A different location may have less congestion or better performance.

Not every streaming problem comes from the VPN. Hotel and airport networks can slow down when many people share the same connection. First, check the underlying Wi-Fi. Then, reconnect to the VPN or try another server.

Closing apps that are downloading files, backing up photos or running large updates can also help. If the connection still struggles, lower the video quality. HD and 4K video require much more bandwidth than standard-definition video. A trusted mobile connection may also perform better than crowded public Wi-Fi, depending on your roaming plan and signal strength.

THE TRICK TO SMOOTHER STREAMING AT HOME AND ON THE ROAD

Traveling with a streaming device can make a hotel room feel more like home. However, VPN setup varies depending on the device.

Apple TV: Some VPN providers offer dedicated Apple TV apps that you can install directly on supported models.

Amazon Fire TV and Fire Stick: Many major VPN services offer apps for compatible Fire TV devices.

Roku: Roku does not support traditional VPN apps directly. Instead, you generally need to connect it through a VPN-enabled router or another supported network setup.

Before packing a streaming stick, check whether your hotel television gives you access to an HDMI port. Also, remember that some hotel networks use a browser-based login page. That can make connecting a streaming device more complicated.

A streaming service may license a movie in the U.S. but not in France, Australia or another country. Another broadcaster or streaming company may hold the rights there. As a result, the same account can show a different catalog after you cross a border.

Live sports can be even more complicated because broadcasting rights often vary by market. That is why it helps to check availability before a trip. A VPN can protect your connection and change the location of the VPN server you connect through. However, it cannot change the licensing agreements behind a streaming service.

With so many VPN services available, I would focus on a few practical things. Look for strong encryption, an easy-to-use app, plenty of server locations and support for the devices you plan to bring. If you expect to stream while traveling, also check whether the VPN works well with the streaming services you use and offers servers in the countries you may need.

A VPN encrypts the traffic between your device and the VPN provider's servers, which can add an important layer of privacy when you are using hotel, airport or café Wi-Fi. Before choosing one, check that it supports your phone, computer, tablet and any streaming devices you plan to use. You should also compare how many devices can connect at the same time, especially if you are traveling with family.

I would also look closely at the provider's privacy practices, reputation and independent security audits. Free VPNs can come with limitations such as slower speeds, fewer server choices or questionable data practices, so read the privacy policy before installing one.

Remember that a VPN is a privacy and security tool. You remain responsible for following the terms of your streaming provider and any applicable laws.

For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com/VPN.

Streaming abroad is much easier than it used to be. Still, I would not wait until you land to figure out your setup. Install your VPN and update your streaming apps before leaving home. Sign in ahead of time, too. Then download something for offline viewing so you have a backup when hotel Wi-Fi becomes unreliable. I also like using a VPN on unfamiliar networks because streaming is only part of what we do online while traveling. You may use the same connection for email, travel reservations and other accounts. Finally, remember what a VPN can and cannot do. It can encrypt your connection and let you select the location of the VPN server you use. It cannot promise that every show, channel or game will be available everywhere you travel.
