item.title: The predominant basketball dynasty on Earth is at stake as America's eyes turn to Caitlin Clark's role
item.description: Caitlin Clark's bench role is under scrutiny as Team USA enters the FIBA Women's World Cup knockout stage with its 33-game winning streak at stake.
item.content:encoded:
American dominance is on the line in this second week of September.

The U.S. women's basketball team is among the predominant dynasties in modern international sports, and have won eight consecutive Olympic gold medals and four consecutive World Cups. They have not lost a game at either event since 2006, and three victories in Berlin have extended their World Cup winning streak to 33 games. Their Olympic win streak is at 61 games.

The U.S. has never lost a quarterfinal game in the FIBA Women's World Cup, and they will look to keep that going on Thursday. But they will have to do it with their biggest star in an undefined role.

CAITLIN CLARK AND ANGEL REESE MUST NOW WORK TOGETHER AT WOMEN'S WORLD CUP AS WNBA TAKES A HIGH-STAKES BREAK

Caitlin Clark has come off the bench in all three group stage games for the US. She went from a record-setting 14-point, 11-assist debut against China to scoring just one point and missing every field goal in a career-low game against Italy, as the U.S. nearly suffered a devastating upset.

Clark rebounded with nine points and seven assists in a blowout win against Czechia to close the group stage.

But going into the knockout stage, as France and Belgium have looked more dominant than the U.S., Clark's role will be a subject of higher consequence, both on the court and on social media. Many fans have called for other young stars like Paige Buecker and Angel Reese to start as well.

And as America will look to defend its Olympic dynasty in home soil in 2028, what happens with Clark, Bueckers and Reese in this next week will be the world's last impression of how those three gel until LA28.

Clark's chemistry with her World Cup teammates was on display in a viral video where three other players appeared to point and laugh as she bent her bare feet backward under a bench to hide them from a camera in the locker room. The players laughing included Reese and Fever teammate Aliyah Boston.

Team USA Coach Kara Lawson has used Clark as a change-of-pace guard off the bench. That strategy looked nearly perfect in the opener against China.

Clark entered the game and immediately accelerated the American offense. She finished with 14 points and 11 assists in 25 minutes as the U.S. won 94-61. She did not commit a turnover.

Her 11 assists were the most ever by an American in a Women’s World Cup debut. Clark also became the first player from any country to record at least 10 assists without a turnover in a World Cup game since FIBA began tracking the statistic in 1994.

CAITLIN CLARK VS PAIGE BUECKERS: HOW TWO WHITE WNBA STARS WOUND UP WITH VASTLY DIFFERENT CULTURAL PERCEPTIONS

Clark said that she was prepared to accept a different role than the one she holds with the Indiana Fever after the China game

"Being surrounded by five people who have won gold medals before at the highest level, I try to follow their lead and take every bit of wisdom they try to give me," Clark said, according to FIBA.

Lawson kept Clark on the bench against Italy, but with more frustrating and frightening results for Americans.

Clark played 19 minutes and missed all six of her field-goal attempts. She finished with one point and one assist while committing two turnovers. It marked the first time in her college or WNBA career that she failed to make a field goal.

Lawson then kept Clark on the bench for the final seven minutes. The U.S. relied on its veteran guards as it erased a late deficit and escaped with a 55-52 victory.

The Americans shot 29% and made only two of their 24 attempts from 3-point range. Their 55 points were their fewest in a World Cup game since FIBA introduced the 3-point line in 1984, according to FIBA.

Clark responded against Czechia one day later. She recorded nine points and seven assists off the bench in a 105-64 victory that secured first place in Group D.

Through three games, Clark has produced 24 points and 19 assists.

That decision will carry more weight from this point forward, with higher stakes and tougher competition in the final round.

If the U.S. falls behind late in the quarterfinals, Lawson will have to decide whether to protect the dynasty with the veterans who built it or place the ball in the hands of the player expected to lead its next generation.

Bueckers and Reese have also come off the bench alongside Clark in every game.

The three stars have already spent years colliding in games that helped transform women’s basketball. Clark and Bueckers were teammates on the United States’ 2019 U19 gold-medal team before splitting two NCAA Tournament meetings. UConn won their 2021 Sweet 16 matchup, but Iowa answered with a 71-69 victory in the 2024 Final Four—a game that drew 14.2 million viewers.

Clark and Reese produced the more heated rivalry. Reese helped LSU defeat Clark and Iowa in the 2023 national championship, then celebrated with a hand gesture that sparked a nationwide debate about sportsmanship, race and double standards. Clark got her revenge in the 2024 Elite Eight, recording 41 points and 12 assists as Iowa defeated LSU despite Reese’s 17 points and 20 rebounds.

Reese left college with LSU’s 2023 national title, while Bueckers won her championship with UConn in 2025. Clark never captured the trophy, but she reached consecutive championship games and helped drive the sport to record television audiences. Now the three players who became famous under the brightest lights are trying to win together—and doing so from Team USA’s bench.

So far in the World Cup, Bueckers has been a more consistent scorer than Clark. She matched Clark with 14 points in the opener against China and added four assists and two steals.

She then produced one of the strongest all-around performances for the U.S. during its scare against Italy. Bueckers finished with seven points, five rebounds, two assists, two steals and two blocks in 19 minutes. She also made the Americans’ first 3-pointer after the team missed its first 10 attempts.

item.title: Is the Iran-backed terrorist movement Hezbollah on the ropes in Lebanon?
item.description: Israel's capture of the Ali al-Taher ridge dealt a severe blow to Iran's Axis of Resistance, but experts warn Hezbollah is still rebuilding.
item.content:encoded:
JERUSALEM — With Israel’s stunning capture of the strategically valuable Ali al-Taher ridge in south Lebanon on Sunday, a major Hezbollah and Iran stronghold, the campaign to degrade Tehran’s so-called "Axis of Resistance" suffered a severe blow.

While the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) triumph is not a death blow, it means that the Iranian-regime-backed Hezbollah terrorist movement lost one of its key offensive bases to plan an invasion of Israel.

IDF Lt. Col. (Res.) Sarit Zehavi, the founder and president of the Israel-based Alma Research and Education Center (Alma), told Fox News Digital that "In the past three years Israel has attacked Hezbollah against various areas, for instance, we degraded the amount of rockets and missiles."

EXCLUSIVE: ISRAEL SEIZES VAST IRAN TERROR AXIS ARSENAL WITH SURPRISING FOREIGN ORIGINS

She noted that the IDF has decimated 90% of Hezbollah’s rocket and missile arsenal. Zehavi said, "Today Hezbollah is holding between 10,000 to 15,000 rockets, which is much less than what it used to have. Most of the array of sophisticated missiles, accurate missiles and long-range missiles was either eliminated or neutralized."

She said, "The capability to launch an invasion of thousands of terrorists into Israel which was the plan, and this was the preparedness three years ago. This capability doesn't exist anymore since the IDF is based in South Lebanon along the borderline, preventing Hezbollah from coming back to those places."

In late August, Alma released a widely read analysis on: "Hezbollah – Situation Assessment: From a Large-Scale Terrorist Army to a Persistent Dispersed Threat."

Zehavi, who resides in northern Israel and has experienced Hezbollah’s massive aerial attacks into her region since the Lebanese terrorist movement joined Hamas in its war against Israel, warned that, "As long as Iran supports its main proxy, which is Hezbollah, it will be very difficult to prevent its rebuilding of its military capabilities and with everything that happened in Iran In the past year, Iran still supports Hezbollah."

She noted that Iran still aids Hezbollah via "arms smuggling and money" and "they still put a lot of effort [into] that and the training and the involvement of Iran in Hezbollah in Lebanon. And this must be stopped."

LEBANON ACCUSES IRAN OF INSERTING IRGC TERRORISTS INTO COUNTRY 'UNDER GUISE OF DIPLOMATIC ACTIVITY'

Iran's regime is a state-sponsor of terrorism and Hezbollah’s base is the Shiite community in Lebanon. Radical Shiite Islamism unifies Iran's regime with its chief proxy, Hezbollah, in Lebanon.

Alma, who has a deep knowledge of Hezbollah’s activities, wrote on X on Sunday: "The battle for the Ali al-Taher Ridge is over – the struggle with Hezbollah is not."

According to Zehavi, Hezbollah "today is much more of a guerrilla organization than a terrorist army as it used to be. It is having a lot of difficulties in rebuilding its capabilities… It is dedicated to rebuilding its military capabilities. But it has a lot of challenges along the way with this regard because of the regime change in Syria, because of that fact that it's much more difficult to transfer weapons through the airport in Lebanon and through Syria. But it doesn't mean that it is not happening. They are still trying and some of it do pass."

Hezbollah’s setback was also echoed by Israel TV’s Channel 12 chief political analyst, Amit Segal. He said the Hezbollah base Ali al-Taher was "Just 10 kilometers (just over six miles) from the Israeli border, with a clear view of the Litani and the Israeli Hula Valley, it was the place from which Hezbollah intended to coordinate its own Oct. 7 in the Galilee."

Hezbollah’s ally, the Hamas terrorist organization, invaded Israel nearly three years ago on Oct. 7 and slaughtered over 1,200 people in southern Israel, including more than 40 Americans.

The IDF announced on Sunday that "Soldiers from the 36th Division have operated in recent weeks to clear and neutralize the two underground routes in the Ali al-Taher Ridge area in the Security Zone. The soldiers achieved operational control of the ridge area, both above and below ground, and cleared the area of terrorists. Some of the terrorists were eliminated, while others fled the area."

PENTAGON HOSTS FIRST-EVER ISRAELI–LEBANESE MILITARY TALKS AIMED AT CURBING HEZBOLLAH

The IDF statement added that "Following operations in the underground routes over the past several weeks, their capability to carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF soldiers from within the routes has been neutralized."

Hezbollah official Mahmoud Qamati told a Lebanese podcaster in late August that, "Ali al-Taher is important, but if it is lost it does not mean the end of Hezbollah."

Lebanon’s Deputy Prime Minister Tarek Mitri told an Arab TV station, also in late August, that the Lebanese army was ready to take over the strategic ridge.

He accused Israel of blocking the army due to its own political considerations ahead of Israeli national elections on Oct. 27.

"The problem is not in the Lebanese army’s readiness but in Israel’s stance," he said.

The Trump administration had pushed for Hezbollah to allow Lebanon’s Army to take control of Ali al-Taher. Hezbollah refused the proposed U.S. deal.

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital that "Hizballah has been the primary obstacle to Lebanon's economic recovery, the main blemish on its international reputation, and the biggest threat to the safety and stability of Lebanon. It bears sole responsibility for Israel's presence on Lebanese soil. This is precisely why Hizballah must be disarmed and dismantled."

EXPERTS URGE EXTREME CAUTION ON IRAN'S 'CROWN JEWEL' HEZBOLLAH — TERROR GROUP WITH US BLOOD ON ITS HANDS

The State Department spokesperson added that "Hizballah is drastically weaker than at any point in recent history, which has allowed the Government of Lebanon to outlaw its military activities. We fully support that decision, as do all of our regional partners."

Hanin Ghaddar, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute who focuses on Shia politics throughout the Levant, told Fox News Digital that "Hezbollah is weakened on two levels. They lost a lot of people, commanders and people, and weapons. Today, there is a goal to rebuild this military structure, invest in rebuilding in personnel, infrastructure and weapons. This is their primary goal."

Ghaddar, who is from Lebanon, added the second level of weakness for Hezbollah is the people are divided within the Shiite community. Hezbollah is no longer the father figure. Hezbollah ended with [Hassan] Nasrallah with his assassination. Hezbollah as protector and liberator is no longer there. It is a mix of IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps], Hezbollah and Nabih Berri [ the Shiite speaker of the Lebanese parliament and the president of the Amal movement]."

Ghaddar said the Shiite community in Lebanon is fractured over whether to continue its support for Hezbollah after multiple wars with Israel.  She said it's "divided over whether Hezbollah is the solution. There is where Hezbollah is bleeding. Hezbollah needs the Shiite community for political power."

Ghaddar said that "Hezbollah has managed to get appointments through their allies, Berri and Amal… They have ministries of finance and health ministry… They really wanted appointments in general security and military. They got that. This reflects their strength economically. They are in survival and using power in the state and cash economy to rebuild."

Multiple Fox News Digital press queries sent to the Lebanese Embassy in Washington, D.C., went unanswered.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Ex-DSA member rips Abdul El-Sayed and warns far-left adopting politics of foreign terror org
item.description: A former Democratic Socialists of America member warns Marxists and Leninists have taken over the DSA and rips Abdul El-Sayed as dishonest.
item.content:encoded:
A former member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) who lives in Michigan issued a dire warning against extremism in American politics, and ripped far-left, progressive Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as dishonest and "sanctimonious."

"So, I think that it's up to everyone to not sit on their hands, Democrats, Republicans, Independents, we all need to be out there," Jake Altman told Fox News Digital. "We all need to be supporting candidates who love this country, who want to deliver for Michiganders. We should not be leaning into this sectarian politics. My fear is we've seen the left wing of the Democratic Party import the politics of Hezbollah into the United States, and now we're living with the sectarian aftermath of that."

Altman, who formerly worked for several labor unions, said the DSA began adding fanatical far-left factions, including Marxists and Leninists, around 2014 and 2015. 

He claimed that at the time, similar far-left actors were taking control of labor unions, intending to use well-meaning workers as pawns in a much larger political battle to push the Democratic Party further left. That was about the time he left the movement, which he said has become "very susceptible to extremist takeover."

FORMER DSA MEMBER ALLEGES COMMUNISTS HAVE ‘CAPTURED’ SOCIALIST GROUP, WARNS DEMOCRATIC PARTY IS NEXT

"That's not America," he said. "We want... a broad, tolerant America. We want pluralism here. We don't want to be at each other's throats. I'm just — we have to stand up and say 'no' to this."

Tensions between the DSA and Democratic Party have reached a boiling point — nowhere more evident than in Michigan — where El-Sayed, who has palled around with socialist streamer Hasan Piker on the campaign trail, is facing difficulty rallying the party's moderates in support of his candidacy.

DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN

"So, I've met Abdul several times," said Altman. "I worked very closely with his dad when his dad was union president of the AAUP local I worked for. So I have, you know, I think I have a pretty good read on the guy."

Mohamed El-Sayed, Abdul's father, is an engineering professor at Eastern Michigan University, where he served as president of the school's AAUP chapter and led a faculty strike in 2022.

"When I was at the Democratic Party convention, the recent Democratic Party nominating convention, [Abdul El-Sayed] recognized me," Altman continued, clarifying that he was referring to April's contentious Michigan Democratic Party endorsement convention. "He was working a line that I was standing in, and he recognized me, and he asked me, 'why all the hate?' 'cause I had been critical of the campaign up to that point."

Altman said Abdul El-Sayed told him that his campaign "doesn't do that," apparently claiming that his campaign wasn't engaged in political mudslinging.

EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS

"We see that the guy is not a straight shooter, he's not an honest broker," said Altman. "He, himself, said that his primary opponent, who I was supporting, couldn't string two coherent sentences together. I mean, the idea that he is somehow above it all is just not true. He's the most sanctimonious man in Democratic Party politics, and that's going a long way because there's a lot of sanctimony in that party."

As for the DSA, according to Altman, it is unrecognizable compared to just a decade ago.

"So, you had this older generation that was very tolerant, part of a broader liberal tradition, engaged in a productive way with the Democratic Party, not a destructive way as we see today," Altman explained.

Part of that tradition, he said, was a total rejection of communism. But recently, the party voted to lift its ban on Leninists, allowing the proliferation of extremism among the party ranks.

"We've seen in August 2025 that DSA at the convention voted to remove its prohibition on having Leninists operating within the organization," he said. "I mean, it doesn't get any clearer than this."

He bemoaned current DSA co-Chair Megan Romer, whom he described as a "Marxist-Leninist" and "fan of the Cuban regime."

HOW THE 'LONG MARCH' THROUGH THE INSTITUTIONS LED TO SOCIALIST TAKEOVER OF DEM PARTY: 'NEED TO WAKE UP'

Romer traveled to Cuba last year with a group of 40 far-leftists, where she hyped the communist country as "care-focused vs. production-focused," blamed the United States' blockade for the country's food shortages and mass emigration, and said the country has "the most LGBTQ-friendly constitution in the world."

Meanwhile, Abdul El-Sayed continues his attempts to try to win over moderate Democrats while also campaigning against Republican former congressman Mike Rogers ahead of the crucial 2026 midterms that will determine whether Democrats regain control of either or both chambers of Congress.

Abdul El-Sayed has been dogged by questions about his affiliation with Piker, whom he invited on the campaign trail during primary season. He has refused to condemn Piker, choosing instead to brush him off as a "streamer from California" who has little connection with the Michigan race.

Piker said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11," and has also praised Mao Zedong and Communist China, said capitalists should be murdered in the streets and spewed a litany of antisemitic comments.

Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign.

item.content:encoded:
America had a headline-grabbing milestone this summer. Unfortunately, it wasn’t our America 250 celebration. Rather, it was passing the $40 trillion mark on our national debt.

$40 trillion is a number that is very difficult to get your head wrapped around. It’s more than 120% of our GDP, a ratio that sounds more applicable to an emerging market in crisis than the biggest economy in the world.

While the debt in and of itself is a problem, there are two related issues that are critical. One is the rapid growth in debt accumulation. In 2017, we passed the $20 trillion mark, and less than 10 years later, we doubled that to $40 trillion.

$50 TRILLION IN DEBT IS NOT A DISTANT THREAT. AMERICA IS SPEEDING TOWARDS IT

This begets the second issue, which is the cost to finance all that debt.

We no longer have the "exorbitant privilege" as it is often referred to of countries adding U.S. dollar reserves no matter what, and that means now, investors in our debt, if we can find them, are price-sensitive. In layman’s terms, they are requiring more of a premium to lend the U.S. government money.

‘THE ODYSSEY’ REMINDS US OF THE NIGHTMARE WE ARE LEAVING FOR AMERICAN CHILDREN

Not only are we running very high deficits (both in absolute terms of $2 trillion a year and in terms of deficits/GDP) that need to be financed, but in recent years, the Treasury has been financing our debt for short-term durations. While a bit cheaper, this debt is in constant need of refinancing (not to mention financing this way tends to be more inflationary).

The reality is that the interest we are required to pay on the debt — that is, money we are spending to finance things we have already bought — is larger than our spending on the military and, if things keep going the same way, may one day be the government’s largest expense category.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS HAVE LOTS OF IDEAS, BUT HOW ARE WE SUPPOSED TO PAY FOR THEM?

So, the question that comes up is, what can we do? Is there even a way out of this?

The answer is yes. We obviously have the tools to be able to get a handle on our debt.

TRUMP TASK FORCE IS TACKLING $250 BILLION IN GOVERNMENT FRAUD. IT’S JUST GETTING STARTED

The problem is that we do not have the political will to do so.

This is a "both parties" problem. The federal government takes in more than $5 trillion each year. For scope, that is more than the GDP of every country in the world except the U.S. and China, and about the size of the GDP of Germany.

WASHINGTON REWARDS FAILURE. IT’S TIME TO SEND CAREER POLITICIANS HOME

Yet, our government still overspends by $2 trillion.

Despite this, many of those in government refuse to address the rampant waste, fraud and abuse in the system, which estimates put at a quarter trillion dollars to $1 trillion per year.

BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT

Congress refuses to take steps to revise our entitlement system in a responsible manner.

Because Congress has been so irresponsible for so long, no matter what it does or does not do, Americans will pay the price. But, for politicians, it is easier to blame someone else for enduring inflation than it is to take a political hit over real reform that will have short-term consequences but long-term benefits.

JOHN ADAMS MADE A TERRIFYING PREDICTION. AMERICA IS CLOSE TO PROVING HIM CORRECT

And that comes to the lack of political will. Nothing changes until Congress changes, and if they are not accountable, they have no incentive to do anything other than pass the buck and the blame.

Warren Buffett once said, "I could end the deficit in five minutes. You just pass a law that says that any time there is a deficit of more than 3% of GDP, all sitting members of Congress are ineligible for reelection." I would suggest two changes to this plan. First, change the 3% of GDP deficit target to "any time the budget isn’t balanced," and second, state that it must be done on the cost side, not via raising taxes.

Incentives drive outcomes, and right now, Congress is incentivized in a way that drives bad outcomes for Americans.

If we want to be able to spend on things that matter (like the defense of our nation), stop the erosion of purchasing power and reset the U.S.’ fiscal and national strength, political will must change, or political incentives must be better aligned with outcomes that benefit Americans instead of the politicians themselves.

item.title: GOP faces brutal midterm headwinds as Republicans paint election as ‘competition with communism’
item.description: President Donald Trump headlines the first-ever GOP midterm convention in Dallas as Republicans fight to hold slim congressional majorities amid inflation.
item.content:encoded:
DALLAS — With less than two months to go until the midterm elections, President Donald Trump and Republicans gather in Texas this week for the first ever GOP midterm convention, as they aim to energize the party's base to turn out in key races that will determine if Republicans keep control of Congress.

Democrats and Republicans traditionally hold large nominating conventions during presidential election years. But Trump a year ago floated the idea of a similar gathering ahead of the midterms, to showcase the signature policy achievements he and the Republicans in Congress produced the past two years.

The president called the convention "a truly Historic Event" and "a RALLY like none other!" when he announced it earlier this summer.

Trump will be at the American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas for the convention's Wednesday and Thursday evening sessions. Trump will speak on both nights, and will deliver the keynote address on the first night, with Vice President JD Vance headlining the second night.

SPEAKER JOHNSON'S MIDTERM PREDICTION TO BUCK HISTORY

The convention comes as Republicans face energized Democrats and stiff political headwinds as they defend their slim House and Senate majorities. There are concerns that the two-day confab that's been described by GOP leaders as a "Trumpapalooza" may not be the best approach with the president's approval ratings deep underwater.

But Republicans are expected to paint a contrast, as they use the convention to spotlight the Democrats' leftward lurch and tie the entire Democratic Party to far-left and socialist proposals.

"This is not a midterm like any other, because we actually have a competition against communism now, and that's a very serious thing. It's going to animate voters coast to coast," House Speaker Mike Johnson emphasized in a Fox News Digital campaign trail interview last month.

Democrats, as they try to win back congressional majorities, were already battling a brand that public opinion polling indicates is extremely unpopular. Making matters worse, the high-profile victories this spring and summer by left-wing and socialist candidates over establishment rivals in Democratic primaries, which gave Republicans extra ammunition to portray all Democrats as extremists.

THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE

"What we're going to highlight at that convention is the fact that this is not your father's Democrat Party," Johnson said. "It's a contrast election, and people are making a contrast between common-sense solutions and candidates, and really crazy, which is represented by the other side."

But Republicans have their own issues.

As the party currently in power, the GOP was already up against traditional political headwinds that have historically led to a loss of congressional seats during midterm election years. Add to that the challenging climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see daily at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's negative numbers.

"Democrats are going to win back power," Democratic National Committee (DNC) Chair Ken Martin predicted last month at the party's summer meeting as he looked towards the midterms.

But his counterpart, Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters, told Fox News Digital this summer, "We have a chance to defy history and win the midterms."

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

The victories by Trump and Republicans two years ago in winning back the White House and Senate and holding the House were fueled by Americans fed up with the high cost of living. Two years later, inflation is the Republicans' biggest liability.

Three out of four voters questioned in the most recent Fox News national poll said inflation had caused financial hardship, while 54% expected the economy to worsen.

"Donald Trump started a war that no one wanted, and now Americans are paying the price. Gas prices are soaring and families who were already struggling in Trump’s economy are forced to stretch their budgets even further while footing the bill for this war," the DNC's Martin charged.

But Gruters and other GOP leaders are spotlighting the major tax cuts on tips, overtime and Social Security that congressional Republicans passed and Trump signed into law last year.

"This midterm convention gives us a chance, an opportunity to showcase all the great things this president has done, and this administration, to the American people in a direct way," he said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

But Republicans are facing a low-propensity problem: MAGA voters who don't always go to the polls when Trump's name isn't on the ballot.

Gruters called Trump the "best showman that's ever existed in politics, bar none... He knows how to deliver these low-propensity voters. He knows how to get people up, motivated, excited about the midterms, and that's what we're going to need."

Johnson, painting a preview of the convention, told Fox News Digital: "Two nights of earned media on every station in America. We'll parade all of our stars across the stage, talk about our extraordinary record of achievement. The president will look into the camera at the end and say, ‘I am on the ballot,’ because we need his base to turn out."

The DNC, which remains in debt and decided against holding a similar convention, sees the GOP confab as a chance to blast Republicans.

"While everyday Americans struggle to pay their bills, fill up their tanks, or put food on the table, Republicans are hosting a multi-million dollar celebration to satisfy an aging and erratic Trump and tie vulnerable Republican candidates closer to his failed agenda," DNC Rapid Response Director Kendall Witmer charged.

Witmer argued that "Americans don’t want a ‘Trumpapalooza’ — they want lower costs and affordable healthcare."

STATE OF PLAY: WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS

Veteran Republican strategist Doug Heye said the GOP convention isn't a bad idea.

But Heye, a former RNC communications director, said "the implementation is important. If it’s Trumpapalooza and 'America has never been hotter or richer,' it will fall flat. If they can be focused on what they’ve done and are doing to lower prices, that, along with fundraising, could have some success."

But he cautioned, "everything we’ve seen thus far suggests the focus will be on Trump, not on the issues voters are screaming about."

In the midterm battle, Republicans come into the convention with a major campaign cash advantage over the Democrats.

"We have a ton of money to spend," Gruters told Fox Business last week. "We have the cash, and we're going to deploy it in a way to make sure that we hold the majority."

And Republicans aim to pad their war chest, as they plan to raise millions of dollars this week during the convention.

That includes asking donors to fork more than $88,000 for a photo with the president at a private roundtable, according to an invitation first reported by the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by Fox News Digital.

Among the other major speakers at the convention: Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Medicaid and Medicare Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner, former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son who's popular among MAGA supporters.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) will be addressing the convention, but his Senate counterpart, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota), is notably absent from the list of speakers released by the RNC.

But a source familiar tells Fox News Digital that Thune will be in Dallas, with a full schedule that includes helping Senate candidates fundraise.
